Role of ESR in Health & Disease

ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, Westergren method) is a non-specific marker of inflammation — measures the rate at which red cells fall in anticoagulated blood over 1 hour. Three stages: rouleaux formation (0-10 min), settling (10-40 min), packing (40-60 min).

Physiological Variations (Health)

  • Normal — 0-15 mm/h (men); 0-20 mm/h (women); higher in elderly (<30 men, <35 women) and in pregnancy (up to 40 mm/h in 3rd trimester).
  • Higher in females, during menstruation, after exercise, with anaemia, advancing age, obesity.

Pathological — Increase

  • Infections — TB, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, pyogenic infections.
  • Inflammation / autoimmune — rheumatoid arthritis (disease activity), SLE, polymyalgia rheumatica, giant cell arteritis (often >100), vasculitis, IBD.
  • Malignancy — multiple myeloma (very high), lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.
  • Tissue necrosis — MI, malignancy, surgery, trauma, burns.
  • Chronic renal failure, nephrotic syndrome — ↑ fibrinogen, ↑ globulins.
  • Hyperthyroidism, hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus.

Pathological — Decrease

  • Polycythaemia vera, severe leucocytosis.
  • Abnormal RBC shape — sickle cell disease, spherocytosis, acanthocytosis.
  • Hypofibrinogenaemia (DIC, severe liver disease), hypogammaglobulinaemia.
  • Congestive heart failure, severe dehydration, shock.
  • Drugs — steroids, salicylates, quinine.
  • Cryoglobulinaemia, technical errors (tilt, delayed test).

Clinical Pearl

ESR trends track disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, giant-cell arteritis, multiple myeloma, and TB. CRP rises & falls faster (hours vs days) and is preferred for monitoring acute inflammation. Markedly high ESR (>100 mm/h) — think myeloma, polymyalgia / temporal arteritis, occult malignancy, chronic infection.

Causes of Pancytopenia

Pancytopenia — simultaneous reduction of all three blood cell lineages (RBC, WBC, platelets). Indicates either decreased production, increased peripheral destruction, or sequestration.

MechanismCauses
Decreased production • Aplastic anaemia (idiopathic, drugs — chloramphenicol/NSAIDs/chemotherapy; viruses — EBV/CMV/HBV/parvovirus B19; radiation; PNH; idiopathic 50%)
• Bone marrow infiltration — leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma, myelodysplasia, myelofibrosis, metastatic carcinoma (breast, prostate, lung), miliary TB, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)
• Megaloblastic anaemia (B12 / folate deficiency) — ineffective haematopoiesis
• Severe iron deficiency (rare)
• Radiation, chemotherapy
• Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH)
• Storage diseases — Gaucher, Niemann-Pick
Increased peripheral destruction • Hypersplenism — portal hypertension, congestive splenomegaly, storage diseases, infections (malaria, kala-azar)
• Autoimmune — SLE, Evans syndrome (AIHA + ITP)
• Microangiopathic — DIC, TTP, HUS
• Infections — severe sepsis, viral haemorrhagic fevers (dengue), brucellosis
• Drugs — chemotherapy, linezolid, immunosuppressants
Sequestration / dilution • Splenic sequestration — massive splenomegaly
• Dilutional — massive fluid resuscitation, massive transfusion
Inherited • Fanconi anaemia (autosomal recessive, DNA repair)
• Dyskeratosis congenita (telomere disorder)
• Shwachman-Diamond syndrome
• Pearson syndrome

Clinical Pearl

Approach to pancytopenia — CBC + peripheral smear + reticulocyte count (low — production defect; high — destruction) → bone marrow aspiration & biopsy. Megaloblastic marrow (giant metamyelocytes) is reversible with B12/folate — always exclude before considering aplastic anaemia. Aplastic anaemia marrow — hypocellular with fatty replacement.

Types of Haemophilia & Investigations

Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder due to deficiency of clotting factor.

Types

TypeDeficient FactorInheritanceFrequency
Haemophilia AFactor VIIIX-linked recessive (Xq28), F8 gene — intron 22 inversion (45% of severe), point mutations, deletions1 in 5,000 male births; 80-85% of all haemophilia
Haemophilia B (Christmas disease)Factor IXX-linked recessive (Xq27), F9 gene — point mutations common1 in 30,000 male births; 15-20%
Haemophilia CFactor XIAutosomal recessive (4q35), F11 gene; common in Ashkenazi JewsRare; mild bleeding
ParahaemophiliaFactor VAutosomal recessiveVery rare
Factor VII deficiencyFactor VIIAutosomal recessiveRare; variable bleeding

Severity Grading

  • Severe — factor <1% of normal; spontaneous bleeding (haemarthrosis, muscle bleeds, intracranial).
  • Moderate — factor 1-5%; bleeding with minor trauma / surgery.
  • Mild — factor 5-40%; bleeding only after major trauma / surgery / dental work.

Laboratory Investigations

  • Screening tests
    • CBC — anaemia after bleed; normal platelet count.
    • Bleeding time — normal (platelet function intact).
    • PT — normal (extrinsic pathway intact).
    • aPTT — prolonged (intrinsic pathway affected).
    • Thrombin time — normal.
  • Specific factor assays
    • Factor VIII assay (haemophilia A) — reduced.
    • Factor IX assay (haemophilia B) — reduced.
    • vWF antigen & ristocetin cofactor assay — normal (differentiates from von Willebrand disease).
    • Factor VIII inhibitor screen (Bethesda assay) — for patients developing inhibitors (alloantibodies), especially severe haemophilia A.
  • Mixing study (correction test) — patient plasma mixed 1:1 with normal pooled plasma — if aPTT corrects → factor deficiency; if does not correct → inhibitor present.
  • Molecular / genetic testing — F8 intron 22 inversion; F9 mutations; carrier detection & prenatal diagnosis.
  • Imaging — ultrasound / MRI of joints (haemarthrosis), CT brain (intracranial bleed).

Clinical Pearl

Treatment — factor replacement therapy (recombinant or plasma-derived factor VIII / IX concentrate) on demand or as prophylaxis; DDAVP (desmopressin) for mild haemophilia A — releases vWF & factor VIII from endothelial stores. Emicizumab (bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIIIa) is a breakthrough subcutaneous prophylaxis for haemophilia A with or without inhibitors. Avoid IM injections, NSAIDs, antiplatelets — use paracetamol for analgesia.

Etiopathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis

RA is a chronic, systemic, autoimmune inflammatory disease primarily affecting synovial joints — characterised by proliferative synovitis, pannus formation, cartilage & bone destruction, systemic features.

Etiology (Multifactorial)

  • Genetic — HLA-DRB1 alleles (shared epitope — "SE"): HLA-DR4 (60-70% in Caucasians), HLA-DR1, HLA-DR10. PTPN22, STAT4, PADI4, CTLA4 polymorphisms. Concordance in monozygotic twins ~15%.
  • Environmental — cigarette smoking (most important; especially in HLA-DR shared epitope — 20× risk), silica exposure, obesity, infections (EBV, parvovirus B19, mycoplasma, Porphyromonas gingivalis — periodontitis), microbiome (gut & lung). Female : male 3:1; hormonal (oestrogens & pregnancy ameliorate; post-partum flares).
  • Autoantibodies — rheumatoid factor (IgM anti-Fc of IgG, 70-80%); anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP — 70-80%, highly specific ~95%, predictive); anti-CarP (anti-carbamylated protein).

Pathogenesis

  1. Citrullination — environmental trigger (smoking, infection) in genetically susceptible host → peptidylarginine deiminase (PADI) enzymes convert arginine to citrulline in synovial proteins.
  2. Loss of tolerance — antigen-presenting cells (HLA-DR shared epitope) present citrullinated peptides to CD4+ T cells → activation of Th1 & Th17.
  3. B-cell activation — produces rheumatoid factor & anti-CCP antibodies; immune complexes form.
  4. Synovial inflammation — activated macrophages & synoviocytes release TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17, IL-23, RANKL → recruit neutrophils, T-cells, B-cells, plasma cells into synovium.
  5. Pannus formation — proliferating synoviocytes, fibroblasts, macrophages & inflammatory cells form a tumour-like mass that invades cartilage & bone.
  6. Cartilage & bone destruction — RANKL activates osteoclasts → bone erosions; MMPs, cathepsins degrade cartilage & proteoglycans; chondrocyte apoptosis.
  7. Systemic inflammation — cytokines enter circulation → fever, fatigue, anaemia of chronic disease, acute-phase response (CRP, ESR), amyloidosis (AA) in chronic untreated cases.
flowchart TD A[Genetic: HLA-DR4 + smoking + infection] --> B[Protein citrullination in synovium] B --> C[Loss of tolerance - CD4 T-cell activation] C --> D[B-cell activation: RF, anti-CCP] C --> E[Macrophage/synoviocyte cytokines TNF, IL-1, IL-6, IL-17] D --> F[Immune complexes in synovium] E --> F F --> G[Pannus formation - proliferative synovitis] G --> H[RANKL → osteoclast activation → erosions] G --> I[MMPs → cartilage destruction]

Clinical Pearl

Anti-CCP antibody is the most specific marker (95%) — appears years before clinical onset; useful in early arthritis. Treat-to-target strategy with synthetic (methotrexate first-line) and biological DMARDs (TNF inhibitors — infliximab, etanercept, adalimumab; IL-6 — tocilizumab; B-cell — rituximab; T-cell co-stimulation — abatacept) has revolutionised outcomes. JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib) — oral small molecules.

Fibroadenoma of Breast

Most common benign breast tumour in young women (15-35 yr); arises from intralobular fibrous & epithelial tissue — a fibroepithelial neoplasm.

Morphological Features

Gross

  • Well-circumscribed, round or ovoid, firm, rubbery nodule; 1-5 cm; freely mobile ("breast mouse" / "mouse in breast").
  • Grey-white to tan cut surface with slit-like clefts & small cystic spaces; bulging surface.
  • Encapsulated; easily enucleated; no haemorrhage or necrosis.
  • Some have myxoid degeneration (especially in adolescent or in pregnancy).
  • Infarction & calcification may occur in long-standing lesions.

Microscopy

  • Circumscribed; pushes adjacent tissue; no infiltration.
  • Two components — (1) benign proliferation of intralobular stroma (fibroblasts & myxoid matrix); (2) benign epithelial proliferation of ducts / terminal duct-lobular units.
  • Two classic growth patterns:
    • Pericanalicular — stroma surrounds ducts in a circumferential pattern; ducts remain round / oval; common in younger women.
    • Intracanalicular — stroma compresses ducts into slit-like clefts; ducts appear stretched; stroma proliferates into duct lumen.
    • Mixed pattern is common.
  • Epithelium — usually double-layered (inner luminal columnar / cuboidal, outer myoepithelial); may show apocrine metaplasia, squamous metaplasia, cystic change, hyperplasia (without atypia).
  • Stroma — varies from cellular & myxoid (young) to hyalinised & acellular (older); occasionally smooth muscle, fat, cartilage, bone metaplasia.

Variants

  • Juvenile fibroadenoma — adolescent girls; rapid growth; cellular stroma; pericanalicular pattern; may be large.
  • Giant fibroadenoma — >5 cm or >500 g; common in adolescents; rapid growth.
  • Complex fibroadenoma — contains cysts >3 mm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, apocrine metaplasia; slight ↑ risk of subsequent carcinoma.
  • Phyllodes tumour — leaf-like projection of stroma into cystic spaces; cellular stroma; benign / borderline / malignant spectrum; behaves differently.

Clinical Pearl

Fibroadenoma is hormone-dependent — often enlarges during pregnancy, lactation, or with OCPs; usually regresses after menopause. Diagnosis — clinical examination + ultrasound (well-defined hypoechoic mass) + FNA / core biopsy. Conservative follow-up acceptable in young women with classic features. Excision if symptomatic, enlarging, suspicious features, or patient preference. Malignant transformation is exceedingly rare (<0.1%).

Krukenberg Tumour

A Krukenberg tumour is a metastatic signet-ring adenocarcinoma to the ovary, typically bilateral, containing mucin-secreting signet-ring cells in a cellular stroma. Strictly, it is a specific histological type of ovarian metastasis — not all ovarian metastases are Krukenberg.

Primary Sites

  • Stomach (gastric adenocarcinoma — signet ring type / linitis plastica) — most common (~70%).
  • Colon & appendix (~15%).
  • Breast (especially lobular carcinoma) — often occult.
  • Biliary tract, pancreas.
  • Rare — small intestine, cervix, bladder.

Route of Spread

  • Transcoelomic (peritoneal) — most common; gravity-dependent pouch of Douglas → ovaries.
  • Haematogenous.
  • Lymphatic (retrograde through para-aortic & pelvic nodes).
  • Direct extension from adjacent viscera.

Morphology

Gross

  • Bilateral in 70-80% of cases.
  • Enlarged, rounded, ovoid or kidney-shaped ovaries; intact capsule; usually 5-10 cm (may be larger).
  • Cut surface — solid, fleshy, grey-white to yellow-tan; may show areas of haemorrhage, necrosis, gelatinous mucin.
  • Often freely mobile — preserving ovarian shape.

Microscopy

  • Signet-ring cells — large cells with intracytoplasmic mucin (clear vacuole) compressing nucleus to one side.
  • Signet-ring cells diffusely infiltrate ovarian stroma — which is cellular, sarcoma-like (spindle cells, often luteinised stromal cells — may produce oestrogen → hormonal symptoms).
  • Mucin pools; PAS positive (diastase resistant); mucicarmine positive; Alcian blue positive.
  • Architecture — diffuse infiltrate; may form glands / cords / nests; classical "Krukenberg" pattern — signet-ring cells within a proliferating stroma.
  • IHC — CK7+, CK20 variable (gastric & colon often CK20+), CDX2+ (intestinal primaries); GCDFP-15 / GATA3 for breast; PAX8 negative (rules out primary ovarian mucinous carcinoma).

Clinical Features

Usually present with abdominal distension, palpable adnexal masses, ascites, weight loss; younger age group than primary ovarian cancer. Hormonal effects — virilisation, postmenopausal bleeding due to stromal luteinisation. Often the primary (stomach / breast) is occult and detected only after ovarian metastasis.

Clinical Pearl

Always suspect Krukenberg in a woman with bilateral solid ovarian masses and ascites — perform upper GI endoscopy, colonoscopy, mammogram, and serum CEA / CA 19-9. Treatment is of the primary tumour; cytoreductive surgery + systemic chemotherapy. Prognosis is poor (median survival <1 year for advanced cases) — the ovarian tumour often is the first sign of an occult primary.

Chronic Pyelonephritis

Chronic tubulointerstitial inflammation & scarring of the kidney due to recurrent or persistent bacterial infection, often associated with vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) or obstruction.

Etiopathogenesis

  • Reflux nephropathy (most common) — vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) since childhood allows infected urine to reflux into renal pelvis & calyces; high-pressure reflux drives infection into renal parenchyma through ducts of Bellini → chronic inflammation, scarring.
  • Chronic obstruction — stones, BPH, prostate cancer, urethral stricture, neurogenic bladder, congenital PUJ obstruction.
  • Recurrent acute pyelonephritis — episodes leave scars.
  • Other predisposing factors — diabetes mellitus, pregnancy, immunosuppression, sickle cell trait, analgesic abuse, intravenous drug use.
  • Pathogens — E. coli (most common), Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus; in chronic — polymicrobial.

Morphology

Gross

  • Kidney is asymmetrically contracted with irregular, coarse, U-shaped cortical scars overlying dilated, blunted calyces.
  • Scars are most prominent at upper & lower poles (where renal papillae are most susceptible to reflux injury).
  • Capsule strips with difficulty due to adherence; surface is granular & depressed.
  • Pelvis & calyces dilated, thickened, with blunted renal papillae; may show calculi.
  • Unilateral or bilateral; one kidney may be more severely affected.

Microscopy

  • Patchy interstitial fibrosis with chronic inflammatory infiltrate — lymphocytes, plasma cells, occasional neutrophils & eosinophils.
  • Tubular atrophy & dilation — dilated tubules contain eosinophilic proteinaceous casts — "thyroidisation" of tubules (resemble thyroid follicles).
  • Glomeruli — periglomerular fibrosis ("crown of thorns"), segmental / global glomerulosclerosis in advanced disease.
  • Arterioles — intimal thickening, hyaline arteriolosclerosis (due to associated hypertension).
  • Pelvic & calyceal urothelium — hypertrophic, congested, with chronic inflammation; may show squamous metaplasia.
  • Acute inflammatory component may be present during exacerbations.
  • Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (variant) — lipid-laden foamy macrophages (xanthoma cells), destructive mass-like lesion, often with obstructing stone; mimics RCC.

Clinical Features

Recurrent UTIs, flank pain, fever, hypertension, polyuria, nocturia (impaired concentrating ability), sterile pyuria, proteinuria (usually <1 g/day), progressive renal failure. Anaemia of chronic disease. Some patients asymptomatic until ESRD.

Clinical Pearl

Coarse cortical scar overlying a dilated calyx is the radiological hallmark — differentiates chronic pyelonephritis from other causes of chronic kidney disease. Ultrasound / CT — small asymmetric kidney with cortical thinning & calyceal blunting. DMSA scan is gold standard for renal scarring. Management — antibiotics for acute exacerbations, treat obstruction & reflux, control BP, monitor renal function; nephrectomy for unilateral non-functioning kidney.

Always send tumour tissue for molecular profiling (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK, KRAS G12C).

Importance of Informed Consent

Informed consent is the process by which a patient is informed about — and voluntarily agrees to — a proposed medical intervention. It is both an ethical imperative and a legal requirement, grounded in the principle of patient autonomy.

Essential Elements of Valid Consent

  1. Capacity / competence — patient must be able to understand, appreciate, reason & communicate a choice.
  2. Disclosure — diagnosis, proposed procedure, alternatives (including no treatment), expected benefits, material risks (physical, psychological, social), prognosis, costs, name of operating surgeon, anaesthesia plan.
  3. Comprehension — information given in language & format the patient understands (interpreter if needed).
  4. Voluntariness — patient must be free from coercion, undue influence, or manipulation.
  5. Decision — patient consents or refuses.
  6. Documentation — signed form, plus note in medical record of the discussion.

Importance

  • Ethical — respects patient autonomy; upholds dignity, freedom, & self-determination.
  • Legal — battery / assault if touched without consent; negligence if risks not disclosed (Bolam test in India / UK — reasonable doctor; Montgomery test — reasonable patient standard).
  • Trust — strengthens physician-patient relationship; sets realistic expectations.
  • Improves outcomes — informed patients comply better, recover faster, less anxious.
  • Protects physician — documentation of consent is a defence in malpractice suits.
  • Research ethics — mandatory for any clinical research under ICMR / Declaration of Helsinki.
  • MCI / NMC Code of Ethics — consent mandatory before any invasive procedure, transfusion, anaesthesia, surgery, HIV testing, sterilisation, organ donation, clinical trial, medical photography, video recording.

Exceptions

  • Emergency — life-saving treatment without consent if patient unconscious & no surrogate available.
  • Therapeutic privilege — withholding information if disclosure would seriously harm patient (rare; ethically contentious).
  • Legal compulsion — court-ordered treatment.
  • Public health — mandatory reporting / quarantine in certain infectious diseases.
  • Waiver — patient explicitly asks not to be informed.

Special Situations

  • Minors — parental consent; assent of child ≥7 years; mature minor doctrine for some decisions.
  • Mentally incapacitated adults — surrogate decision-maker; Mental Healthcare Act 2017 — advance directive.
  • Pregnant woman — her autonomy prevails even if refusal may harm fetus.
  • Research / clinical trials — Ethics Committee approval + written informed consent mandatory (ICMR 2017).

Clinical Pearl

Consent is a process, not a form. The signed form is documentation, not the consent itself — what matters is the discussion. Disclose material risks — those that a reasonable patient would want to know (Montgomery test, replacing older Bolam test). Always record the discussion, the patient's questions, and the decision in the medical record.

Leukocytosis — WBC count >11,000/μL. Classified by predominant cell type.

TypeCausesLab Findings
Neutrophilic leukocytosis (>7,000/μL or >75%) Bacterial infections (pyogenic — Staph, Strep, pneumococcus); tissue necrosis (MI, burns, trauma); acute haemorrhage / haemolysis; leukaemia (CML); corticosteroids; lithium; pregnancy; exercise; stress; eclampsia; gout; ketoacidosis Neutrophilia with left shift (band cells), toxic granules, Döhle bodies, cytoplasmic vacuoles in sepsis; LAP score high (leukemoid) vs low (CML)
Lymphocytosis (>4,000/μL adult or >8,000 child) Viral infections — EBV (infectious mononucleosis), CMV, HIV, pertussis, measles, hepatitis, mumps, rubella, influenza; chronic infections — TB, brucellosis, syphilis; lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL, ALL); hyperthyroidism; Addison disease; chronic lymphocytic proliferative disorders Atypical lymphocytes (reactive — Downey type I-III) in EBV; smear cells in CLL; flow cytometry for clonality

Investigations — General Approach

  1. CBC with differential count; peripheral smear (morphology — toxic changes, atypical cells, immature forms).
  2. C-reactive protein, ESR, procalcitonin (bacterial).
  3. Blood cultures, urine culture, swab & cultures from suspected focus.
  4. Serology — viral (EBV, CMV, HIV, HBV, HCV), autoimmune (ANA, RF), parasitic (IgE, stool).
  5. LAP score (leukemoid vs CML); BCR-ABL / Philadelphia chromosome; flow cytometry (clonality); bone marrow if leukaemia suspected.
  6. Imaging — chest X-ray, ultrasound; CT scan for occult abscess / malignancy.

Clinical Pearl

Leukemoid reaction (WBC >50,000 with marked left shift from infection / inflammation) mimics CML. Differentiate by — high LAP score (leukemoid), toxic granulation, no Philadelphia chromosome, no basophilia, primary infection identifiable. CML — low LAP, Ph+ chromosome, basophilia, splenomegaly, BCR-ABL transcript.

Introduction (½ mark)

Gastric carcinoma is a malignant epithelial neoplasm arising from the glandular epithelium of the gastric mucosa. It is the fifth most common cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer-related death. Adenocarcinoma constitutes ~95% of all gastric malignancies. Two distinct epidemiological patterns exist: the intestinal type (environmental, epidemic, distal stomach, older patients) and the diffuse type (genetic, sporadic, proximal/body, younger patients, signet-ring morphology).

Etiology / Risk Factors (1½ marks)

CategoryRisk Factors
InfectionHelicobacter pylori (Class I carcinogen — chronic atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma); EBV (≈9% of gastric cancers)
DietaryHigh salt, smoked/cured foods (nitrosamines), pickled vegetables, low intake of fresh fruits & vegetables, aflatoxin, poor refrigeration
Host / geneticBlood group A; hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1/E-cadherin mutation); Lynch syndrome (MSH2/MLH1); Peutz-Jeghers (STK11); familial adenomatous polyposis
Premalignant conditionsChronic atrophic gastritis with intestinal metaplasia; gastric adenoma (>2 cm); Ménétrier disease; post-gastrectomy stump (>20 yr); pernicious anaemia
Environmental / lifestyleSmoking, alcohol, obesity (proximal cancers), low socio-economic status, radiation exposure

Morphology — Gross (1 mark)

Bormann classification (advanced carcinoma):

  • Type I — polypoid / fungating mass projecting into lumen.
  • Type II — ulcerating with raised, indurated margins ("everted edges").
  • Type III — ulcerated & infiltrating into wall (most common).
  • Type IV — diffusely infiltrating (linitis plastica — "leather-bottle stomach"), thickened rigid wall without discrete mass.

Early gastric cancer (confined to mucosa/submucosa irrespective of nodes): Paris classification — Type IIc (depressed), IIa (elevated), IIb (flat), I (protruded).

Morphology — Microscopic (1 mark)

Lauren classification:

  • Intestinal type — cohesive glandular structures, apical mucin, intestinal metaplasia in surrounding mucosa, expansive growth, haematogenous spread.
  • Diffuse type — scattered single signet-ring cells (mucin-displaced nucleus), poorly cohesive, infiltrative growth, transmural & serosal spread, peritoneal deposits; CDH1 mutation.
  • Mixed / indeterminate type.

Other variants: papillary, tubular, mucinous (colloid), hepatoid, adenosquamous, parietal-cell. Spread: direct (pancreas, transverse colon, liver); lymphatic (left supraclavicular — Virchow node / Troisier sign, periumbilical — Sister Mary Joseph nodule, ovary — Krukenberg tumour); haematogenous (liver, lung, bone); transcoelomic (Blumer shelf, rectal shelf of Douglas).

Clinical Pearl

The Correa cascade describes the multistep pathogenesis of intestinal-type gastric carcinoma: chronic gastritis → atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma — a process driven over 20–30 years by H. pylori. Eradication of H. pylori before dysplasia develops can interrupt this cascade, which is why H. pylori screening and treatment is now part of gastric cancer prevention strategies in high-prevalence regions like Japan and Korea.

Definition (½ mark)

Atherosclerosis is a chronic, progressive, lipid-driven inflammatory disease of large and medium-sized elastic and muscular arteries, characterised by intimal deposition of lipids, complex carbohydrates, blood products, fibrous tissue and calcium — forming atheromatous plaques that narrow the lumen and predispose to thrombosis, aneurysm, and distal ischaemia.

Risk Factors / Etiology (1 mark)

  • Non-modifiable — age, male sex, post-menopausal females, family history, genetic dyslipidaemias (familial hypercholesterolaemia — LDLR, PCSK9, APOB).
  • Modifiable (major) — hypercholesterolaemia (↑LDL, ↓HDL), hypertension, smoking, diabetes mellitus.
  • Modifiable (minor) — obesity, physical inactivity, atherogenic diet, hyperhomocysteinaemia, post-menopausal hormone therapy, chronic kidney disease, HIV infection / anti-retroviral therapy, systemic lupus erythematosus, periodontitis, air pollution.

Pathogenesis — Response-to-Injury Hypothesis (1½ marks)

  1. Endothelial injury / dysfunction — hypertension, turbulent flow, toxins (smoking), hyperlipidaemia, hyperglycaemia, homocysteine → reduced NO bioavailability, increased permeability, adhesion molecule expression (VCAM-1, ICAM-1, E-selectin).
  2. Lipoprotein entry & modification — LDL crosses dysfunctional endothelium → accumulates in intima → oxidised by ROS & enzymes (MPO, 15-LO) → oxLDL is atherogenic & immunogenic.
  3. Monocyte adhesion & diapedesis — monocytes bind VCAM-1, enter intima, differentiate into macrophages via M-CSF.
  4. Foam-cell formation — macrophage scavenger receptors (SR-A, CD36, LOX-1) take up oxLDL (unregulated, not feedback-inhibited) → cytoplasm stuffed with lipid droplets → foam cells → form fatty streaks (earliest visible lesion, yellow, flat).
  5. Platelet adhesion & smooth muscle recruitment — platelets adhere, release PDGF; activated macrophages & T-cells secrete cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IFN-γ) & growth factors (PDGF, FGF, TGF-β) → recruit & proliferate medial smooth muscle cells → migrate into intima (synthetic phenotype).
  6. Plaque maturation — SMCs synthesise extracellular matrix (collagen, elastin, proteoglycans) forming a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich necrotic core (deceased foam cells, cholesterol clefts, calcification).
  7. Neovascularisation & calcification — vasa vasorum grow into plaque, prone to rupture → intraplaque haemorrhage; MGP, osteopontin drive calcification.

Morphology (1 mark)

  • Fatty streak — yellow, flat intimal streak; lipid-laden foam cells; reversible; appears in childhood.
  • Fibrous plaque / atheroma — white-yellow, raised, eccentric; fibrous cap (SMCs + collagen) over necrotic core with cholesterol clefts, foam cells, lymphocytes.
  • Complicated plaque — calcification, ulceration/rupture, haemorrhage, thrombosis, aneurysmal dilation.

Pathophysiology / Consequences

  • Stable narrowing → chronic stable ischaemia (angina, claudication).
  • Plaque rupture / erosion → exposes thrombogenic core → platelet aggregation & thrombus → acute arterial occlusion → MI, stroke, sudden death.
  • Weakening of media → aneurysm (aortic).

Clinical Pearl

The vulnerable (unstable) plaque — not the tightly stenotic one — usually causes acute MI: a thin fibrous cap (<65 µm), large lipid-rich necrotic core, heavy macrophage infiltration, high MMP activity, and outward (positive) remodelling make it rupture-prone. Because it remodels outward, the lumen remains near-normal on angiography — explaining why ~70% of MIs originate from lesions that were previously <50% stenotic. This is the rationale for aggressive lipid-lowering (statins stabilise plaques) independent of stenosis severity.

Overview

Ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) are the two major idiopathic inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD). Differentiation on biopsy/colectomy is critical because it dictates medical & surgical management.

Feature Ulcerative Colitis Crohn's Disease
Gross siteColon + rectum only; continuous from rectum proximallyAny part of GI tract mouth→anus; terminal ileum most common
PatternContinuous, circumferential, proximal extensionSkip lesions, segmental, cobble-stoned mucosa, discontinuity
Rectal involvementAlways (proctitis → pancolitis)Often sparing of rectum
Wall characterThinned, shortened, loss of haustra ("lead-pipe" on barium)Thickened, rigid, "hose-pipe" / "string sign" on barium
Inflammation depthMucosal & submucosal onlyTransmural (full thickness)
Mucosal surfaceBroad-based shallow ulcers; pseudopolyps (islands of regenerating mucosa)Deep linear / aphthous ulcers, fissures, cobblestone appearance
MicroscopyCrypt abscesses (neutrophils in crypt lumens), crypt architectural distortion, mucin depletion, Paneth cell metaplasiaNon-caseating granulomas (~30–50%), transmural lymphoid aggregates, fissuring ulcers, skip areas
Fat wrappingAbsentPresent (creeping fat)
Fistulae / fissuresRareCommon (perianal fistula, enterovesical, enterocutaneous)
StricturesRare (consider cancer)Common
Serologyp-ANCA positive (≈70%)Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibody (ASCA) positive
SmokingProtective (ex-smokers at risk)Aggravates risk
SurgeryCurative — proctocolectomy removes diseaseNot curative — recurrence at anastomosis common
Cancer riskHigher (after 8–10 yr of pancolitis)Lower, but present in long-standing colonic disease
ComplicationsToxic megacolon, perforation, colorectal carcinoma, primary sclerosing cholangitisObstruction, fistulae, abscess, malabsorption, B12 deficiency, gallstones, kidney stones

Clinical Pearl

The single best discriminator on histology is the non-caseating granuloma — pathognomonic of Crohn's when present, though only seen in 30–50% of cases. When granulomas are absent, look for transmural inflammation and skip lesions. The coexistence of primary sclerosing cholangitis strongly favours ulcerative colitis — this association is so consistent that PSC patients should undergo annual colonoscopy regardless of symptoms. Remember the mnemonic: Crohn's = Cobblestone, Continuous-skip, Constriction, Creeping-fat, Cholonic-sparing of rectum.
